claims.claim: A bond is a debt security, like an IOU: borrowers issue bonds to raise money from investors willing to lend for a set amount of time, and buying a bond means lending to the issuer — a government, municipality, or corporation.
The issuer promises to pay a specified rate of interest during the life of the bond and to repay the principal, also known as face value, when the bond matures.
Bonds typically pay interest on a regular schedule, such as every six months; bonds held to maturity return the entire principal and are described as a way to preserve capital while investing.
Bonds can help offset exposure to more volatile stock holdings.
Credit (default) risk is the risk that the issuer fails to make its interest or principal payments on time and in the worst case defaults on its bonds.

Interest-rate risk: changes in interest rates can affect a bond's value before maturity; if sold before maturity the bond may be worth more or less than face value, and rising rates can force an older lower-rate bond to be sold at a discount.
A stock is a type of security that gives the holder a share of ownership in a company, which is the contrast to a bond, where the holder is a lender.

U.S. Treasury securities are issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury and are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States government; Investor.gov calls them a safe and popular investment.
A marketable security can be transferred to someone else and sold before it matures.
Treasury Bonds pay interest every six months and are long-term: historically a 30-year investment, now also offered in 20-year terms (U.S. context).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether bonds can be described as 'safe'
positions: Investor.gov calls U.S. Treasuries 'a safe and popular investment'
the same page lists credit risk, interest-rate risk, inflation risk, liquidity risk, and call risk for bonds generally
TreasuryDirect notes all Treasury marketable securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson separates the two: Treasury securities carry very low default risk because of the full faith and credit backing, but all bonds — Treasuries included — carry interest-rate risk. The lesson uses 'calmer' and 'low default risk,' never 'risk-free.'

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether bonds are 'less risky' than stocks
positions: Investor.gov says bonds can help offset exposure to more volatile stock holdings
bonds carry their own named risks (credit, interest-rate, inflation, liquidity, call)
the finance subject owns formal risk comparison
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the general role — bonds as the steadier companion to stocks — without claiming any particular bond is safe or that bonds always outperform.

positions: Investor.gov's FAQ describes Treasury Bonds as long-term securities that typically mature in 30 years
TreasuryDirect says they are historically a 30-year investment, now offered in 20-year terms as well
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the TreasuryDirect description (long-term; interest every six months; 20- and 30-year terms) and does not state a single fixed term.
